common_name: Gold Cone Juniper (Narrow Columnar Golden-Foliage Juniper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; golden foliage color is strongest and growth stays tightest with full sun, while light shade fades the color and loosens the columnar habit.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, since this narrow columnar juniper is intolerant of wet feet and develops its brightest gold color and tightest form with maximum light. Gold Cone is a sport of common juniper selected for a strongly upright, slender columnar habit and soft golden-yellow new growth that mellows to yellow-green with age, making it a popular vertical accent for narrow beds, foundation corners, and formal plantings where space is tight. It needs essentially no pruning to hold its naturally tidy spire shape and tolerates drought, wind, and poor soil once established, though it performs best in climates with a real winter chill and can struggle with humid, mild-winter heat. Avoid overhead watering and crowding, which encourage the fungal blights that trouble junipers in humid regions.

common_name: Sixteen Candles Summersweet (Dwarf Fragrant White-Flowered Clethra for Shade)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Sixteen Candles tolerates wet soil and heavy shade better than most flowering shrubs, making it a reliable choice for damp shaded beds.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and mulch well to keep the shallow roots cool and consistently damp through summer heat. Sixteen Candles is a compact selection of native summersweet bred for dense, upright flower spikes that stand out from the foliage like small white candles, blooming in mid- to late summer with an intense, sweet fragrance that draws bees and butterflies from a distance. Its tolerance for wet, poorly drained soil and heavy shade makes it one of the more useful flowering shrubs for low spots, rain gardens, and woodland edges where few other shrubs bloom well, and its compact size suits smaller foundation plantings better than full-sized summersweet cultivars. Established plants sucker gently to form a dense colony over time and need little more than an occasional thinning of old canes to stay vigorous.

common_name: Chewings Fescue (Fine-Bladed Bunching Cool-Season Turf and Shade Grass)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 4–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm seedbed in shade to partial sun; Chewings fescue is among the most shade-tolerant of the fine fescues, making it a standard component of shade lawn and woodland-edge seed mixes.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed 1/4 inch deep into a firm, well-prepared seedbed, keeping the surface consistently moist until germination. Chewings fescue is a fine-bladed, bunch-type cool-season grass valued for exceptional shade tolerance, low fertility needs, and the ability to establish under tree canopies where turf-type tall fescue and bluegrass struggle, making it a mainstay of shade lawn mixes, woodland-edge plantings, and low-input groundcover under widely spaced orchard or landscape trees. Once established it needs little mowing or fertilizer and tolerates drought and poor, acidic soils better than most turf grasses, though it does not tolerate heavy foot traffic or extended summer heat and humidity as well as warm-season lawn grasses. In mixed seedings it is typically combined with creeping red fescue and other shade-tolerant species to build a dense, low-maintenance sod for shaded areas.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Chewings Fescue

common_name: Hard Fescue (Slow-Growing Low-Maintenance Shade- and Drought-Tolerant Grass)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 4–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm seedbed in light shade to full sun; hard fescue's slow, low growth habit and deep roots suit unmowed slopes, roadsides, and naturalized shade edges where mowing is difficult.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed 1/4 inch deep into a firm seedbed, keeping the surface moist through germination and light establishment mowing. Hard fescue is a fine-textured, slow-growing bunchgrass prized for the lowest maintenance needs among the fine fescues, thriving with minimal mowing, fertility, or water once established and tolerating both dry, infertile soil and moderate shade better than almost any other cool-season turf species. Its deep, tough root system and slow top growth make it especially useful for erosion control on slopes, low-mow or no-mow naturalized areas, and shaded woodland edges under trees, where it forms a persistent, fine-textured sod that resists weed encroachment. It is less tolerant of heavy foot traffic and hot, humid summers than turf-type fescues, so it is most reliable in cooler climates or as a low-input groundcover rather than an active-use lawn.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Hard Fescue

common_name: Sheep Fescue (Fine-Bladed Bunchgrass for Dry Shade and Poor Soil)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 4–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm seedbed in light shade to full sun; sheep fescue's dense, wiry bunching habit and tolerance for thin, dry, infertile soil suit it to slopes, roadsides, and dry shaded ground under trees.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed 1/4 inch deep into a firm seedbed, keeping the surface moist through germination and the first mowing or two. Sheep fescue is a fine, wiry-leaved bunchgrass closely related to hard fescue, valued for thriving on the thinnest, driest, most infertile soils where few other grasses persist, and for tolerating light to moderate shade along woodland edges and under widely spaced trees. Its tight bunching habit and blue-green color make it useful as an accent or low-mow groundcover as well as a practical erosion-control and soil-stabilizing species on dry slopes and roadside cuts. Like other fine fescues it struggles with heavy foot traffic, waterlogged soil, and the combination of high heat and humidity, so it is best suited to cooler climates or as an unmowed naturalized planting rather than an active-use lawn in the Deep South.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Sheep Fescue
